# OneCoin / “Cryptoqueen” Network: Reconstruction of the Publicly Documented Fraud Scheme

## Executive summary

The publicly documented evidence describes OneCoin as an international investment-fraud scheme structured around the marketing and sale of a purported cryptocurrency through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. The scheme operated from approximately 2014 through 2019, was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, and generated more than $4 billion in investments from victims worldwide, according to the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). The principal founders identified in the supplied sources are Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. The DOJ describes both as co-founders who, together with others, orchestrated the scheme; a secondary legal publication identifies Greenwood as the network’s leading MLM distributor and describes his role in promoting OneCoin and earning commissions from sales ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The evidence supports a distinction between established enforcement outcomes and unresolved matters. Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000, according to the ArentFox Schiff summary of the U.S. prosecution. The DOJ separately reports that more than $40 million in forfeited assets is available for victim compensation through a remission process. These amounts should not be treated as contradictory: the sources do not say that the $300,000 figure represents the total pool of forfeited assets available to all OneCoin victims ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison); [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

Ruja Ignatova’s status remains unresolved in the supplied evidence. The DOJ states that she remains an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and that investigators continue efforts to locate her. The evidence does not establish whether she is alive, dead, in hiding, or being protected by other persons. Accordingly, claims about her death, current location, or alleged associates would go beyond the supplied sources and should not be presented as facts ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

## Scope and source assessment

This report relies exclusively on two supplied sources:

1. An April 13, 2026 DOJ press release describing the OneCoin remission process, the alleged scheme, the government investigation, and the continuing fugitive status of Ignatova.
2. A September 15, 2023 ArentFox Schiff Investigations Blog article summarizing Greenwood’s sentencing and several factual allegations presented by prosecutors.

The DOJ source is the more authoritative source for current enforcement information, victim compensation, the government’s description of the scheme, and Ignatova’s current legal status. The ArentFox Schiff article is a secondary source, but it provides additional detail about Greenwood’s sentence, his alleged position as OneCoin’s leading MLM distributor, the alleged mechanics of the cryptocurrency representations, and the amount of forfeiture attributed to him. Where the secondary source reports prosecutorial allegations, those allegations are labeled as such rather than treated as independently established facts.

## Reconstruction of the OneCoin scheme

### Formation, location, and operating period

According to the DOJ, OneCoin began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. The scheme marketed and sold a cryptocurrency called “OneCoin” through a global MLM network. The DOJ identifies Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood as co-founders and states that they, along with others, orchestrated the investment scheme between 2014 and 2019 ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The ArentFox Schiff account is consistent with this chronology. It states that OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and began operating in the United States around 2015. It also reports that the government charged Greenwood and others with obtaining more than $4 billion in investments from approximately 3.5 million investors through alleged misrepresentations about OneCoin ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The available evidence therefore supports the following timeline:

| Period | Publicly documented event | Evidentiary status |
|---|---|---|
| 2014 | OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria | Reported by DOJ and secondary source |
| Around 2015 | OneCoin began operating in the United States | Reported by ArentFox Schiff |
| 2014–2019 | The alleged investment-fraud activity and victim purchases occurred | DOJ identifies this period for eligible purchases |
| June 2022 | Ignatova was added to the FBI Top Ten Most Wanted List | Reported by DOJ and ArentFox Schiff |
| September 2023 | Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison | Reported by ArentFox Schiff |
| April 2026 | DOJ announced a remission process for eligible victims | DOJ enforcement and compensation fact |

## Principal founders and roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identifies Ruja Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin and describes her as one of the principal individuals who, together with Greenwood and others, orchestrated the international investment scheme. The source does not provide a detailed organizational title beyond co-founder, nor does it specify a particular technical, financial, or marketing function attributable solely to Ignatova ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The DOJ further states that Ignatova remains an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and that the FBI continues to pursue information concerning her whereabouts. This is an enforcement-status fact, not proof of any particular theory about what happened to her. The supplied sources do not confirm her location or physical condition. They also do not establish that she has been convicted, sentenced, or apprehended ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

The sources identify Karl Sebastian Greenwood as OneCoin’s other co-founder. The DOJ describes him as a co-founder involved in orchestrating the scheme. The ArentFox Schiff article provides a more specific description of his operational role, stating that prosecutors characterized Greenwood as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor. According to that account, he allegedly earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, amounting to more than $300 million ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The ArentFox Schiff account reports that Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. Unlike several statements in the article that are expressly framed as allegations or prosecutorial descriptions, the sentence itself is presented as an enforcement outcome. On the evidence supplied, Greenwood is the only OneCoin principal for whom the sources report a completed criminal sentence ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

## Alleged mechanics of the fraud

### Marketing through an MLM network

The core distribution mechanism was an international MLM structure. The DOJ states that OneCoin marketed its purported cryptocurrency through a global MLM network. The ArentFox Schiff article explains that members received commissions for recruiting other people to purchase cryptocurrency packages. This structure allegedly enabled the scheme to expand through personal recruitment and sales incentives rather than through a conventional public cryptocurrency market ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The evidence supports describing MLM recruitment and package sales as central features of the scheme. It does not, however, identify every distributor, corporate affiliate, promoter, or regional network participant. Nor does it establish from the supplied material that every purchaser knew the investment was fraudulent or that every participant acted with criminal intent.

### Misrepresentations concerning value and market operation

The ArentFox Schiff account reports that prosecutors alleged OneCoin falsely represented that its value was determined by market supply and demand. According to the reported allegations, the value was instead set arbitrarily and without regard to market forces. This is an allegation attributed to the government’s case and should not be broadened into a claim about every statement made by every OneCoin promoter ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The DOJ’s description is more general: it states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide as a result of misrepresentations concerning OneCoin. The DOJ does not enumerate every alleged false statement in the supplied press release, but its account is consistent with the secondary source’s description of deceptive representations about the product and its value ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

### Alleged absence of a verifiable blockchain

The ArentFox Schiff article reports that Greenwood claimed OneCoin had a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions. Prosecutors allegedly maintained that no public, verifiable blockchain existed. This distinction is significant because the representation of a functioning blockchain was apparently used to support the credibility of the product as a cryptocurrency. However, the supplied source presents this as part of the government’s allegations summarized in the article; the report should therefore retain that qualification ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

### Scale of victimization

The DOJ reports that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide. The ArentFox Schiff article adds an estimate of approximately 3.5 million investors. These figures describe the reported scale of the scheme, but the sources do not provide a country-by-country breakdown, a verified list of victims, or a distinction between gross purchases and net losses ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

## Enforcement and victim-compensation developments

The DOJ states that the Southern District of New York brought several OneCoin-related prosecutions. It further reports that several key figures have been sentenced and that the government pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the alleged fraud. More than $40 million in forfeited assets was reported as available for victim compensation as of the April 2026 announcement ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The remission process is intended for individuals who purchased OneCoin between 2014 and 2019 and may be eligible for compensation. The DOJ identifies Kroll Settlement Administration LLC as the remission administrator and states that the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the process. The announced petition deadline is June 30; the supplied text does not specify the year, so it should not be inferred from the source alone ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The DOJ expressly warns that neither the remission administrator nor the department will ask victims to pay to participate. This warning is especially relevant because victims of an earlier fraud may be targeted by secondary “recovery” scams. The supplied DOJ material directs potential victims to the official remission website and telephone number, but this report does not independently verify those contact details beyond reproducing the source’s information ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

## Enforcement facts versus unresolved claims

| Issue | Supported conclusion | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| OneCoin’s principal founders | Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood are identified as co-founders | Enforcement-source fact |
| OneCoin’s business model | Global MLM distribution and sale of purported cryptocurrency packages | DOJ description; supported fact |
| Total reported investment | More than $4 billion worldwide | DOJ-reported figure |
| Estimated investor population | Approximately 3.5 million | Secondary-source report |
| Greenwood’s sentence | 20 years in prison | Reported enforcement outcome |
| Greenwood’s forfeiture | Approximately $300,000 | Reported enforcement outcome |
| Victim-compensation pool | More than $40 million in forfeited assets available | DOJ-reported current compensation fact |
| Ignatova’s status | FBI Top Ten Fugitive; efforts to locate her continue | Current enforcement status |
| Ignatova’s whereabouts | Not established in supplied sources | Unresolved |
| Whether Ignatova is alive | Not established in supplied sources | Unresolved |
| Claims about secret protectors or associates | Not established in supplied sources | Unsupported and omitted |
| Alleged false blockchain and valuation representations | Reported prosecutorial allegations | Allegation, not independently expanded here |

## Assessment

On the supplied evidence, the most defensible conclusion is that OneCoin was not merely an unsuccessful cryptocurrency project but an alleged international investment-fraud operation organized around deceptive representations, MLM recruitment, and sales of cryptocurrency packages. The criminal enforcement record is strongest with respect to Greenwood: the sources report a completed 20-year sentence and forfeiture order. The broader scheme is documented by the DOJ as involving Ignatova, Greenwood, and others, but the supplied material does not provide equivalent final judicial outcomes for every participant.

Ignatova’s status must be treated with particular caution. The evidence establishes that she is wanted by the FBI and remains at large from the perspective of the supplied DOJ account. It does not resolve the competing possibilities concerning her location or fate. A responsible OSINT assessment should therefore describe her as an unresolved fugitive subject, not as confirmed dead, confirmed alive in a particular location, or definitively protected by named individuals.

## References

ArentFox Schiff. (2023, September 15). *Co-founder of fraudulent cryptocurrency sentenced to 20 years in prison*. ArentFox Schiff. [https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs. (2026, April 13). *Justice Department announces compensation process for OneCoin fraud victims with funds recovered through asset forfeiture*. [https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact. Dearington Share This Page Email LinkedIn X Facebook Headlines that Matter for Companies and Executives in Regulated Industries Off Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison Karl Sebastian Greenwood, a citizen of Sweden and the United Kingdom and co-founder of the cryptocurrency OneCoin, was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his alleged role in a $4 billion fraud scheme. As described by prosecutors, OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency with the same name through a multi-level-marketing (MLM) scheme. Around 2015, OneCoin began operating in the United States. The government charged Greenwood and others with making various misrepresentations about OneCoin to secure over $4 billion in investments from approximately 3.5 million investors. These alleged misrepresentations include claiming that OneCoin’s value was based on market supply and demand though the value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces. Greenwood also claimed to have a private blockchain to identify OneCoins and record historical transactions, when no public verifiable blockchain actually existed. According to the government, OneCoin marketed its cryptocurrency through a global MLM network whereby OneCoin members would receive commissions for recruiting others to purchase cryptocurrency packages. As OneCoin’s top MLM distributor, Greenwood is alleged to have earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling over $300 million. In addition to his 20-year prison term, Greenwood was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. OneCoin’s other co-founder, Ruja Ignatova, remains at large and was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. A link to the US Department of Justice’s (DOJ) press release can be found here. Prison Inmate Pleads Guilty in COVID-19 Relief Fraud Telvin Breaux, an inmate in a California prison, and three other co-defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy and aggravated identity theft charges for their alleged roles in a $25 million unemployment benefits scheme. According to the DOJ, Breaux and his co-defendants obtained personal identifying information of other inmates, as well as patients and customers at hospitals, dentists’ offices, and other businesses where one of the co-defendants worked or had connections. Breaux and his co-defendants then used this information to submit fraudulent unemployment insurance claims to the California Employment Development Department (EDD). In connection with these false claims, Breaux and his co-defendants also made specific misrepresentations that the individuals whose information they stole were unable to work as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. In total, defendants are alleged to have submitted over 400 fraudulent claims totaling over $25 million to the EDD, $5.4 million of which was actually paid out and used by the defendants to purchase luxury vehicles, fund trips to Las Vegas, and pay rent and tuition. Each defendant faces a maximum of 22 years imprisonment as well as fines of $250,000. A link to the DOJ’s press release can be found here. Former NYC Non-Profit Finance Director Sentenced to 18 Months Imprisonment Donna Murray, the former finance director of a New York City-based nonprofit financial services trade association with over 600 members, was sentenced to 18 months imprisonment for allegedly embezzling nearly half a million dollars from the nonprofit. The government alleges that Murray was the nonprofit’s sole finance department employee and was responsible for maintaining the organization’s books and records, handling accounts receivable and payable, and managing financial statements to outside auditors. In addition, Murray is alleged to have been the only employee with the ability to make wire transfers for the organization. As detailed in the DOJ’s information, Murray was charged with a months-long embezzlement scheme in which she stole over $488,000 from the organization’s bank accounts through 105 unauthorized wire transfers to her personal account. Murray covered up the scheme by creating false entries in the organizations general ledger and transferring less than $10,000 in each transaction to avoid triggering bank reporting requirements. Prosecutors charged Murray with using the misappropriated funds to pay personal loans and purchase luxury items. For her conduct, Murray was sentenced to 18 months in prison. Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact.
